titulo: Autonomy by evidence, not by trust
lead: The temptation is to grant autonomy early: the answers look good and someone says "just let it run on its own." It's like promoting the intern on day two because they asked a good question. This lesson gives you the four levels, the numbers to move up, and the way back.
objetivo: decide when to raise or lower an agent's autonomy level using accuracy, run volume, and the severity of errors.

aprende.t: The four levels: recommends, executes with approval, executes with exceptions, operates within limits
The numbers to move up a level
When to step down, and why it isn't punishment
Practice the conversation with someone who wants to skip steps

hero_alt: Driving school practice track seen from above, with a car and orange cones.

secoes.sub: One task at a time. Click each level to see the criteria for moving up.

nos.detalhe: The agent analyzes and suggests; you evaluate, decide, and do it. Start of operation, high-risk scenario, or no history. Every agent starts here.

nos.sub: Nothing goes out without an OK
nos.detalhe: The agent does the work and leaves it pending; the human approves each action. To move up to here: accuracy above 90% at level 1, at least 50 evaluated runs, and zero serious errors in the last 2 weeks.

Common cases go out on their own; new scenarios, high amounts, and rule conflicts go to review. To move up: above 95% at level 2, 200 evaluated runs, zero serious errors in the last month, and interventions below 5%.
Autonomous within clear limits: maximum amount, types of decision, hours, scope. To move up: above 98% at level 3, 500 evaluated runs, zero serious errors in 2 months, and tested limits.

secoes.legenda: The criterion for moving up isn't a suggestion: it's a requirement. Without the numbers, the promotion doesn't happen.
secoes.dica: The same ladder applies to everything: personal life, Jarvis, and your business. The kits, skills, and project packages use these four levels.

secoes.sub: Eight metrics. The first three are the minimum.

texto: History of runs in that scenario and accuracy rate by evaluation (human or automated).
Not every error is equal: getting the tone of a message wrong is not the same as getting the amount on an invoice wrong. How much does each failure cost in money, time, reputation, or rework?
Does the rate hold over time or swing? Does it keep quality across varied scenarios, not just simple ones? How often does someone need to correct it?
If an agent at level 3 starts making mistakes in a new way (the scenario changed, a rule is outdated, an integration broke), it moves down to level 2 until it stabilizes.
Moving down isn't punishment. It's the cycle working.

secoes.titulo: Simulated conversation: the director in a hurry
secoes.sub: A simulated conversation for practice. Pick the answer you would give; the comment appears right after.

personagem.papel: wants the leads agent sending emails on its own

abre.cliente: The lead qualification agent has been great for a week. I want it to send the follow-up emails on its own starting Monday. Can you release it?

opcoes.t: Sure. If the answers are good, we save time.
opcoes.comenta: Autonomy based on trust. "Looks good" is not a number, and sending outside the company is exactly the kind of action that needs a track record first.

opcoes.t: Before I release it: how many runs have been evaluated, and what's the accuracy rate?
opcoes.comenta: Right question. The decision comes from the numbers, and you didn't say yes or no before seeing them.

opcoes.t: I think it's too early, but you're the one who decides.
opcoes.comenta: Your instinct is right, but it's opinion against opinion. Without asking for the numbers, the conversation becomes a contest of confidence.

numeros.cliente: About 40, I think. The team skimmed them and liked them. One email went out with an old price, but it was just one.

opcoes.t: Then it goes straight to level 3: it sends and the team reviews only the exceptions.
opcoes.comenta: That skipped two steps. With 40 runs and a price error, not even level 2 is cleared.

opcoes.t: Let's go to level 2: it prepares the email and nothing goes out without approval.
opcoes.comenta: Safer, but still too early: level 2 requires at least 50 evaluated runs and zero serious errors in the last two weeks. The old price is a serious error.

opcoes.t: A wrong price for a customer is a serious error. It stays at level 1, the team sends, and we fix the context: a price table with an expiration date.
opcoes.comenta: Exactly. You rated the severity, kept the level, and turned the failure into the smallest possible fix, in the environment.

criterio.cliente: Okay. But when does it move up? I don't want to be stuck here forever.

opcoes.comenta: A criterion nobody can check. A month from now the same conversation comes back, and whoever is in more of a hurry wins.

opcoes.t: A month from now, if nobody complains.
opcoes.comenta: There's a deadline, but "nobody complains" isn't an evaluation. Without a reviewed sample, an error nobody saw counts as a success.

opcoes.t: When there are 50 evaluated runs, accuracy above 90%, and zero serious errors in the last two weeks. I'll put that in the scorecard and we'll look at it together.
opcoes.comenta: A written, verifiable criterion with a date to review it. His hurry becomes a goal he can track himself.

fim-pressa.texto: The next wrong email (old price, wrong recipient, a promised deadline) will go out to the customer without anyone seeing it. Promoting without numbers is a gamble. Start over and try to decide by the data.

fim-vago.texto: You held the level, but without a written number the promotion comes down to who pushes hardest. Start over and give a criterion that can be checked.

fim-bom.texto: The agent stays at level 1, the failure became a context fix, and the promotion has a written criterion in the scorecard. When the numbers arrive, the decision is easy, for both of you.

secoes.licao: Ask for the numbers, rate the severity of the error, hold the level, and write the criterion for moving up. The hurry becomes a goal.

secoes.sub: Copy this into the agent profile, one table per task.

blocos.conteudo:
## Autonomy — task: <e.g.: send follow-up>
Current level: 1 (recommends; human decides and executes)   since: <date>

To move up to level 2 (executes with approval):
- [ ] 50+ evaluated runs        today: 
- [ ] accuracy above 90%            today: 
- [ ] zero serious errors in 2 weeks   last serious error: 

A serious error on this task is: <e.g.: wrong price, deadline, or recipient>
Moves down one level if: a new serious error appears or accuracy drops below <x>%
Next review: <date>

exercicios.texto: Pick one task for your agent (personal, Jarvis, or company) and fill in the promotion criterion. Define what a serious error is for it.
exercicios.pronto: the profile has the current level, the three numbers to move up, what a serious error is, and the rule for moving down.

exercicios.titulo: 2 · Simulated conversation with a top score
exercicios.texto: Do this lesson's simulated conversation. If you don't reach the top score, read the comments and start over.
exercicios.pronto: you finished with the top score and you can say why "wrong price" kept the agent at level 1.

perguntas.p: An agent has 120 evaluated runs at level 1, 93% accuracy, and no serious errors for three weeks. Can it move up?
perguntas.explica: It meets all three level 2 criteria (90%+, 50+ evaluated, zero serious errors in 2 weeks). Level 3 requires 95%+ at level 2 and 200 evaluated.

perguntas.p: An agent at level 3 starts making mistakes because the CRM integration changed. What should you do?
opcoes: Keep it at level 3 and hope for the best
Move it down to level 2 until it stabilizes
Shut the agent down for good
perguntas.explica: The way back down is part of the cycle. Move down, fix the environment, measure, and move up again when the numbers return.

perguntas.p: Why separate the severity of an error instead of just counting the accuracy rate?
opcoes: Because getting the tone of a message wrong is not the same as getting an invoice amount wrong
Because the accuracy rate doesn't matter
Because the model classifies on its own
perguntas.explica: 97% accuracy with one invoice error can be worse than 90% with tone errors. That's why every level requires zero serious errors.

perguntas.p: What is the difference between level 2 and level 3?
opcoes: At level 2 a human approves every action; at level 3 they only review the exceptions
At level 2 the agent does nothing
At level 3 there is no human
perguntas.explica: At level 2 nothing goes out without an OK. At level 3 the common cases go out on their own and the human oversees the exceptions. Even at level 4 there are reports and limits.

itens.texto: Recommends, executes with approval, executes with exceptions, operates within limits.
90%/50, 95%/200, 98%/500, always with zero serious errors in the period.

itens.t: Moving down is part of it
itens.texto: New error, one level down, until it stabilizes.
